Finally, we can multiply two complex numbers just like multiplying two binomials. Again, we use the fact that [MATH: \mathrm{i}^2=-1.]

Content:
So, to multiply [MATH: 2 + \textrm{i}] and [MATH: 5 + 3\textrm{i},] we proceed as follows:

&= 10 + 6\textrm{i} + 5\textrm{i} +3\textrm{i}^2 \
&= 10 + 11\textrm{i} + 3(-1) \
&= 10 + 11\textrm{i} - 3 \
&= 7 + 11\textrm{i}
}]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Multiplying a purely imaginary number by a real number is similar to multiplying two monomials.

Content:
For example, we can multiply the purely imaginary number [MATH: 3 \textrm{i}] by the real number [MATH: 6] as follows:
[MATH: 6 ⋅ 3\textrm{i}|= (6 ⋅ 3)\textrm{i} = 18\textrm{i}]

Content:
Similarly, we can multiply a complex number by a real number using the distributive property.

Content:
For example, we can multiply the complex number [MATH: 2-3\textrm{i}] by the real number [MATH: 3] as follows:
[MATH: \eqalign{
3(2-3\textrm{i}) &= 3\cdot2 + 3\cdot(-3\textrm{i}) \[3pt]
&= 6 + 3\cdot (-3)\textrm{i} \[3pt]
&= 6 -9\textrm{i}
}]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Multiplying by a Purely Imaginary Number

Content:
Multiplying two purely imaginary numbers is similar to multiplying two monomials. But we also need to use the fact that [MATH: \textrm{i}^2=-1.]

Content:
For example, to multiply [MATH: 2\textrm{i}] and [MATH: 3\textrm{i},] we proceed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (2\textrm{i})(3\textrm{i})|= 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ \textrm{i}^{2}; = 6\textrm{i}^{2}; = 6(− 1); = − 6]

Content:
Knowing this, we can also multiply a complex number by a purely imaginary number.
For instance, to multiply [MATH: 2\textrm{i}] and [MATH: 4-3\textrm{i},] we use the distributive property and the fact that [MATH: \textrm{i}^2=-1\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \eqalign{
2\textrm{i}(4-3\textrm{i})
&= 2\textrm{i}\cdot 4+2\textrm{i}\cdot(-3\textrm{i}) \[3pt]
&=2\cdot 4\textrm{i}+2\cdot(-3)\textrm{i}^2\[3pt]
&= 8\textrm{i}+(-6)(-1)\[3pt]
&= 8\textrm{i}+6\[3pt]

&=6+8\textrm{i}
}]

Item 15 — Tutorial: Multiplying Two Complex Numbers

Content:
Finally, we can multiply two complex numbers just like multiplying two binomials. Again, we use the fact that [MATH: \mathrm{i}^2=-1.]

Content:
So, to multiply [MATH: 2 + \textrm{i}] and [MATH: 5 + 3\textrm{i},] we proceed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
(2+\textrm{i})(5+3\textrm{i}) &= 2 (5+3\textrm{i}) + \textrm{i} (5+3\textrm{i}) \
&= 2\cdot5 + 2\cdot(3\textrm{i}) +\textrm{i}\cdot 5+ \textrm{i} \cdot (3\textrm{i}) \
&= 10 + 6\textrm{i} + 5\textrm{i} +3\textrm{i}^2 \
&= 10 + 11\textrm{i} + 3(-1) \
&= 10 + 11\textrm{i} - 3 \
&= 7 + 11\textrm{i}
}]
